# myArc, forever yours.

An open-source browser bringing back Arc, with no account required and optional AI.

[Download pre-alphaNightly v2026.11.13.4](https://myarc.dev/download/)
[See what works](https://github.com/bitbonsai/myarc#try-it)

## How you browse is part of how you work. It should outlast the company behind your browser.

[Arc is being sunsetted](https://arc.net/), and its code was never open, so nobody can keep it going. **myArc is open source**, so anyone can.

## What we hold to

- ### Yours to keep

  Your workspace stays on your computer, in files you own. Export is on the way.
- ### Keep what worked

  If you used Arc, you already know myArc. Where they differ, onboarding shows you.
- ### AI by choice

  AI is off until you turn it on. Then you pick: a local model, your own API key, or a hosted option, and you decide what it can see.
- ### Built in the open

  The plans and decisions are public too, not just the code. If I stop, anyone can pick it up where I left off.

## Where it stands

[See it full size](https://myarc.dev/product-window-light.webp)[See it full size](https://myarc.dev/product-window-dark.webp)

- ### Works now

  Spaces, pinned tabs and Favorites, the Library, tabs that survive a restart, and AI agents that browse in a Space of their own.
- ### Next, for alpha

  Split view, Little Arc, ad and tracker blocking on by default, and onboarding.
- ### After alpha

  Builds for Windows and Linux.

[Download the 2026.11.13.4 nightly →](https://myarc.dev/download/) [Full alpha checklist →](https://github.com/bitbonsai/myarc/blob/main/docs/ALPHA.md)

## Read along

- [Roadmap](https://github.com/bitbonsai/myarc/blob/main/ROADMAP.md)

  Milestones, dependencies and the gates a release has to pass.
- [Architecture](https://github.com/bitbonsai/myarc/blob/main/docs/ARCHITECTURE.md)

  Why Chromium, and what Rust owns.
- [Arc migration](https://github.com/bitbonsai/myarc/blob/main/docs/MIGRATION.md)

  What an Arc import brings over, what it leaves out, and how export will work.
- [AI and services](https://github.com/bitbonsai/myarc/blob/main/docs/AI.md)

  Provider choices, privacy rules and how a hosted option would be paid for.
- [CLI and MCP control](https://github.com/bitbonsai/myarc/blob/main/docs/CONTROL-PROTOCOL.md)

  How the terminal and AI agents drive the browser, and what you let them do.
- [Contributing](https://github.com/bitbonsai/myarc/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md)

  How to help without drifting from the product.

# Blog

November 2026

## [Letting agents use myArc](https://myarc.dev/blog/agents-use-myarc/)

November 10, 2026

The agents that build myArc can now use it, in a Space of their own and only after you say yes. Getting there turned up a bug in Chromium and a sidebar full of gray globes.

## [One window, two profiles](https://myarc.dev/blog/one-window-two-profiles/)

November 06, 2026

myArc now has real Profiles, so Work and Personal keep their own cookies and logins. Getting them to live in one window, the way Arc did, took more than I expected.

## [Taking a few patches from ungoogled-chromium](https://myarc.dev/blog/ungoogled-chromium/)

November 04, 2026

myArc now borrows four build flags and five patches from ungoogled-chromium. I left out the patches that would cost myArc more than they give, like the ones that break the Chrome Web Store.

## [Chasing Arc's details](https://myarc.dev/blog/closer-to-arc/)

November 01, 2026

Side-by-side recordings showed what myArc's sidebar was missing, and a quit bug was emptying every Space. Next up is an alpha checklist.

October 2026

## [Why myArc is now GPL-3.0](https://myarc.dev/blog/gpl/)

October 29, 2026

myArc moved from the MIT license to GPL-3.0 so it stays open for good. I don't plan to make money from it, and any modified version has to publish its code.

## [Building myArc in public](https://myarc.dev/blog/building-in-public/)

October 25, 2026

Why I'm building myArc after Arc's sunset announcement, with account-free browsing, no behavioral tracking and an Artcraft-inspired workflow.

# myArc pre-alpha nightly

Pre-alpha nightly, for trying the Arc-like shell. Not for daily or sensitive browsing.

[Download for macOS (Apple silicon)](https://github.com/bitbonsai/myarc/releases/download/nightly-2026.11.13.4/myArc-Nightly-2026.11.13.4-arm64.dmg)

- **Version:** 2026.11.13.4
- **Date:** November 13, 2026
- **Size:** 234.2 MB
- **SHA-256:** `0831dab2b8f90a432d84690f459776180a3db48cd124ef18d1d82b8d878cdfd6`

## System requirements

- An Apple silicon Mac. Intel Macs are not supported.
- macOS 26 or later. The glass frame requires macOS 26\. It has been tested only on macOS 26.7.

## First launch

1. Check the download against the SHA-256 listed with it. The two values must match.

   ```
   shasum -a 256 ~/Downloads/myArc-Nightly-2026.11.13.4-arm64.dmg
   ```
2. Open the DMG and drag myArc Nightly to Applications.
3. macOS blocks the first launch because the app is not notarized. Right-click myArc Nightly, choose Open, then Open again. If macOS only offers Done or Move to Trash, which macOS 15 and later usually does, open System Settings \> Privacy \& Security, scroll to the myArc Nightly message and choose Open Anyway.
4. Or remove the quarantine flag in Terminal and open the app normally.

   ```
   xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine "/Applications/myArc Nightly.app"
   ```

## What works today

Each item was seen working in a native run or experiment note. None of it has had release testing.

- Chromium browsing, with Chromium extensions. A Manifest V3 smoke test passed; wider extension coverage is untested.
- A glass sidebar with Favorite tiles, a Space heading, pinned tabs, a New Tab row and temporary tabs below the divider, next to a rounded page card. Only the dark appearance has been compared with Arc.
- Creating, switching and renaming Spaces from the sidebar footer. Favorites are shared across the Spaces of one Profile.
- Closing a pinned tab keeps the pin.
- A command bar: Cmd\+L opens it on the current address, arrows, Enter and Escape work, and new windows open it centered.
- Shortcuts: Cmd\+S hides the sidebar, Cmd\+Shift\+T reopens a closed tab, Cmd\+Shift\+C copies the address and shows a Copied Current URL toast, Cmd\+Shift\+N opens a private window and Ctrl\+Cmd\+N a blank one.
- Cmd\+, opens a native Settings window. General shows the default-browser banner, Profiles sets when tabs are archived, and Advanced holds Import from Arc and a link to the full Chromium settings. Links and Shortcuts are not available yet.
- Quitting with Cmd\+Q needs no confirmation by default, with a setting to turn the warning on.
- Importing an Arc export from Settings \> Advanced \> Import from Arc. A preview shows what it will add, then each Space arrives with its folders and pinned tabs, in Arc's order. Importing the same file again adds nothing.
- Folders for a Space's pinned tabs. Create, rename and delete them from the right-click menu, and open or close them. Drag tabs in and out, and rename a pinned tab from its menu.
- Split View for two tabs side by side. Use Open in Split View in a tab's menu or Ctrl\+Shift\+\=, and Ctrl\+Shift\+- to separate them. The split shows as one sidebar row and comes back after a restart.
- Agents can drive tabs in the Agent Space through the bundled myarc CLI and MCP server. It is off by default. Turn it on in Settings \> Advanced, and myArc asks before each new agent connects.

## Known limitations

- No automatic updates and no security updates. Install each new nightly by hand.
- Not yet notarized by Apple, so macOS blocks the first launch until you allow it.
- Recent tabs and navigation can be lost after a crash or force quit.
- H.264 and AAC are included, so most other web video plays.

[Known limitations](https://myarc.dev/docs/known-limitations/) lists the rest, with what does not work yet and what to do after a crash.

## Other ways to get it

- [GitHub releases](https://github.com/bitbonsai/myarc/releases/tag/nightly-2026.11.13.4) lists every nightly.
- [Source on GitHub](https://github.com/bitbonsai/myarc), with instructions to [build it from source](https://github.com/bitbonsai/myarc/blob/main/browser/README.md).
- [GitHub issues](https://github.com/bitbonsai/myarc/issues) take bug reports. Include the version, your macOS version and the steps that trigger the problem, and leave out private pages.

## License and notices

myArc is licensed under GPL-3.0, see [LICENSE](https://github.com/bitbonsai/myarc/blob/main/LICENSE). Chromium and other bundled components keep their own licenses. [ATTRIBUTION.md](https://github.com/bitbonsai/myarc/blob/main/ATTRIBUTION.md) records what is known, and the [dependency license inventory](https://github.com/bitbonsai/myarc/blob/main/browser/evidence/dependency-licenses.json) is not yet complete.

# Install myArc

What your Mac needs, how to get past the first-launch warning, and how to move to a newer nightly.

myArc ships as a pre-alpha nightly, a build made from the latest code and published without release testing. Each nightly is a disk image (DMG) on the [download page](https://myarc.dev/download/).

## What you need

- A Mac with Apple silicon. Intel Macs aren't supported.
- macOS 26 or later. The glass window frame needs macOS 26, and the nightly has only been tested on macOS 26.7.

## Install the app

1. Download the DMG from the download page.
2. Check the file against the SHA-256 checksum listed next to the download button. Run this in Terminal and compare the two values. They must match. If you kept older nightlies in Downloads, it prints one line per file.

   ```
   shasum -a 256 ~/Downloads/myArc-Nightly-*.dmg
   ```
3. Open the DMG and drag myArc Nightly to Applications.

## First launch

The app is signed with an Apple Developer ID but isn't notarized yet. Notarized means Apple has scanned the build. Without it, Gatekeeper, the part of macOS that checks downloaded apps, blocks the first launch.

To open it anyway, right-click myArc Nightly in Applications, choose Open, then choose Open again. On macOS 15 and later the warning usually offers only Done or Move to Trash. In that case open System Settings \> Privacy \& Security, scroll to the message about myArc Nightly and choose Open Anyway.

You can also remove the quarantine flag in Terminal and then open the app as usual:

```
xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine "/Applications/myArc Nightly.app"
```

macOS may then ask for your login password so myArc can read the key that protects its saved data. Choose Always Allow. Nightlies from 2026.11.03 on are signed with the same Developer ID, so later nightlies stop asking.

## Update to a newer nightly

myArc doesn't update itself, and it gets no security updates between nightlies. To move to a newer one:

1. Quit myArc with Cmd\+Q.
2. Download the new DMG and drag myArc Nightly to Applications, replacing the old copy.
3. Open it. The new download goes through the first-launch step again.

Your Spaces, tabs and settings live in your user folder, outside the app, so replacing the app keeps them. [Your data](https://myarc.dev/docs/your-data/) shows where.

The [GitHub releases page](https://github.com/bitbonsai/myarc/releases) lists every nightly.

[Next: Import from Arc →](https://myarc.dev/docs/import-from-arc/)


---

HTML: https://myarc.dev/docs/import-from-arc/

# Import from Arc

Export your Spaces from Arc, preview what myArc will add, and import them with their folders and pinned tabs. Importing the same file twice adds nothing.

myArc reads the file Arc exports and adds your Spaces and their links to the sidebar. Arc stays untouched, and so does the export file.

## Export from Arc

In Arc, open Settings, go to Advanced and choose Export Data. Arc saves a Markdown file that lists each Space by name, with the links under it.

## Import into myArc

1. Press Cmd\+, to open Settings and go to the Advanced tab.
2. Click Import from Arc and pick the exported file.
3. Read the preview, then click Import. Cancel closes the preview and writes nothing.

The preview counts the Spaces and pinned tabs the import adds and the pinned tabs already in myArc. It also lists links it leaves out and lines it couldn't read. Nothing loads while you import, and each pinned tab opens its page the first time you click it.

## What comes over

- Each Space in the export becomes a Space with the same name, in Arc's order. If a Space with that name already exists, its links go there.
- Each folder in a Space becomes a folder with the same name, and its links become pinned tabs inside it, in the export's order.
- Arc Favorites become pinned tabs at the top of that Space. The export doesn't say which links were Favorites, so myArc can't make them Profile Favorites.
- Only http and https links come over. Anything else shows up under the links left out.

The export holds only Space names and links. Tab titles, Profiles, temporary tabs, archived tabs, themes, history, passwords, cookies, extensions and Boosts aren't in it, so they don't come over. Imported Spaces join the Profile you're using. [Spaces and Profiles](https://myarc.dev/docs/spaces-and-profiles/) explains the difference.

myArc refuses files over 8 MB.

## Import again

Importing the same file a second time adds nothing. myArc reuses Spaces and folders by name and keeps the pinned tabs they already have. Pinned tabs from an import made before myArc had folders move into their folder. If you export from Arc again later, the next import adds only the new Spaces and links.

An import never removes anything. If it fails partway, nothing changes, because myArc tries every import on a copy of your workspace before it writes.

[Next: Spaces and Profiles →](https://myarc.dev/docs/spaces-and-profiles/)


---

HTML: https://myarc.dev/docs/spaces-and-profiles/

# Spaces and Profiles

How Spaces, Profiles, pinned tabs, Favorites and temporary tabs fit together in the myArc sidebar.

myArc keeps Arc's model. A Space sorts your tabs by topic, and a Profile keeps your logins apart. They are separate things, and several Spaces can share one Profile.

## Spaces

A Space is a set of tabs for one part of your life, such as Work, Reading or Travel. Each Space has its own pinned tabs and temporary tabs, and a name, an icon and a color.

- To create a Space, click \+ at the bottom of the sidebar. Give it a name, pick an emoji or icon, choose its Profile and pick a theme color.
- To switch Spaces, click the Space's dot at the bottom of the sidebar.
- To rename the current Space, click its name at the top of the sidebar.

## Profiles

A Profile holds your cookies, logins, history and extensions. Spaces that share a Profile share all of that, plus the Profile's Favorites. A Work Profile and a Personal Profile let you stay signed in to two accounts on the same site.

Each myArc Profile is a full Chromium Profile, so the separation is the same one Chrome gives you. To make a new Profile, open the Profile menu while you create a Space and choose New Profile.

Switching to a Space in another Profile brings in that Profile's window at the same position and size, so it still feels like one window.

## Pinned tabs and Favorites

Pinned tabs and Favorites both appear as favicon tiles at the top of the sidebar, the Favorites first.

- A pinned tab belongs to one Space and shows only there.
- A Favorite belongs to the Profile and shows in every Space of that Profile.

Right-click a tab in the sidebar to pin it to the Space or add it to the Profile's Favorites. The same menu moves a tile between the two, and Unpin from Space or Remove Favorite takes it away.

Closing a pinned tab or a Favorite keeps its tile. The page closes, and clicking the tile opens it again.

## Folders

A folder groups pinned tabs inside a Space. To make one, right-click the Space name at the top of the sidebar and choose New Folder. Right-click a folder to rename or delete it, and click it to open or close it. To file a tab, right-click it and choose Move to Folder. Remove from Folder takes it out again. Folders don't nest.

## Temporary tabs

Every other tab is a temporary tab. Temporary tabs sit in a list below the Space name and the New Tab row. They come back after you quit and reopen myArc.

When you close a temporary tab, it moves to Archived Tabs in the Library. Open the Library with the archive icon at the bottom left of the sidebar. It also lists your Spaces and recent downloads.

## Not in myArc yet

Folders inside folders, dragging a tab up to pin it or into a folder, Peek and Split View don't work yet. [Known limitations](https://myarc.dev/docs/known-limitations/) has the full list.

[Next: Keyboard shortcuts →](https://myarc.dev/docs/shortcuts/)


---

HTML: https://myarc.dev/docs/shortcuts/

# Keyboard shortcuts

The shortcuts that work in myArc today, and the Arc shortcuts that are still missing.

These shortcuts work in the current nightly. Standard Chromium shortcuts, such as Cmd\+W to close a tab and Cmd\+R to reload, work as they do in Chrome.

| Shortcut | What it does | Compared with Arc |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cmd\+T | Opens the command bar for a new tab | Same |
| Cmd\+L | Opens the command bar on the current address | Same |
| Cmd\+S | Hides or shows the sidebar | Same |
| Cmd\+Shift\+C | Copies the current address and shows a Copied Current URL message | Same |
| Cmd\+Shift\+T | Reopens the last closed tab | Same |
| Cmd\+Shift\+N | Opens a private window | Same |
| Ctrl\+Cmd\+N | Opens a blank window | Same |
| Cmd\+, | Opens Settings | Same |
| Cmd\+Q | Quits without asking. Settings \> General has a switch to turn on a warning | Same key |

The command bar is the box for addresses and searches. Inside it, the arrow keys move through suggestions, Enter opens the selected one and Escape closes the bar.

Cmd\+Shift\+C opens the element inspector in Chrome. myArc follows Arc and copies the address instead.

## Arc shortcuts that don't work yet

These belong to features myArc doesn't have yet.

| Shortcut | What it does in Arc |
| --- | --- |
| Cmd\+Option\+N | Opens Little Arc, a small window for a quick page |
| Ctrl\+Shift\+1, Ctrl\+Shift\+2 | Moves focus between the panes of a Split View |
| Cmd\+O | Turns a Peek preview into a tab |

You can't change shortcuts yet. The Shortcuts tab in Settings is greyed out until it's built.

[Next: Your data →](https://myarc.dev/docs/your-data/)


---

HTML: https://myarc.dev/docs/your-data/

# Your data

Where myArc keeps your workspace on disk, how to back it up, and what it sends over the network. There is no account.

myArc has no account and nothing to sign in to. Everything it saves stays on your Mac.

## Where it lives

myArc keeps its data in this folder:

```
~/Library/Application Support/myArc Nightly/
```

Inside it, each Profile has its own folder. The first is called `Default`, later ones `Profile 1`, `Profile 2` and so on. A Profile folder holds Chromium's usual data, such as history, cookies and extensions, plus one myArc file, `myarc-workspace-v1.json`. That file is your workspace, meaning the Spaces of that Profile with their names, icons and colors, your pinned tabs and Favorites, your temporary tabs and Archived Tabs. It's plain JSON you can open in a text editor.

When myArc saves the workspace, it writes a new file and swaps it in, so a save that gets interrupted leaves the previous version in place.

Saved passwords and cookies stay in Chromium's own stores. Chromium encrypts them with a key it keeps in your macOS Keychain, under the name myArc Nightly Safe Storage.

## Back it up

There is no export command yet. To back up everything, quit myArc and copy the whole `myArc Nightly` folder somewhere safe. Quitting first means nothing is halfway through a save while you copy.

## What goes over the network

myArc adds no analytics and no usage tracking. It makes one kind of request of its own. When a pinned tab or Favorite has no icon yet, myArc asks that site for its icon. The request goes only to that site's domain, carries no cookies and never sends the path of the page you saved. No Google icon service or other third party is involved.

Every other request comes from Chromium itself. myArc turns off a few of the ones that go to Google:

- Chromium no longer asks Google's servers for the current time.
- Domain Reliability reports, which Chromium sends Google when a connection to one of its sites fails, are off.
- WebRTC text logs, which video calls can upload for debugging, are off by default.

Crash report uploads are off too. Crash reports stay on your Mac. [Known limitations](https://myarc.dev/docs/known-limitations/) says where to find them.

## Agent control

Agents and scripts can't touch myArc until you turn on Allow agents to control myArc in Settings \> Advanced. Until then myArc writes nothing to its control folder. [CLI and MCP](https://myarc.dev/docs/cli-and-mcp/) covers how it works.

[Next: CLI and MCP →](https://myarc.dev/docs/cli-and-mcp/)


---

HTML: https://myarc.dev/docs/cli-and-mcp/

# CLI and MCP

Drive myArc from a script or an AI agent with the bundled myarc command and its MCP server. It's off by default, and tab commands reach only the Agent Space.

myArc comes with a command-line tool, `myarc`, that drives tabs in the browser. The same tool runs an MCP server, so AI agents such as Claude Code can use the browser too. MCP, the Model Context Protocol, is the standard way AI tools discover and call outside tools.

Agents work in the Agent Space, a Space myArc keeps for them, with a bot icon. They can't see or touch tabs in your other Spaces.

## Turn it on

Browser control is off by default. Press Cmd\+, to open Settings, go to Advanced and turn on Allow agents to control myArc. The switch covers every Profile. Turning it off disconnects every tool at once.

## Install the command

The nightly carries `myarc` inside the app. Link it into your `PATH`:

```
sudo mkdir -p /usr/local/bin
sudo ln -sf "/Applications/myArc Nightly.app/Contents/Helpers/myarc" /usr/local/bin/myarc
```

The link points into the app, so it keeps working after you replace the app with a newer nightly.

## Approve each tool

The first time a tool connects, a card at the top right of your myArc window names the tool and asks whether it may control your Agent Space. Choose Allow or Don't allow. The command waits up to 60 seconds for your answer. Allow lasts until you quit myArc.

While a tool is working, the bot icon at the bottom of the sidebar shows a small blue dot. To take back control, right-click the bot and stop the tool from its menu, or click Stop next to the Agent Space's name. Stop disconnects the tool, and its next command asks you again.

## Short commands

An outline is a text version of the page, one element per line. Anything you can act on carries a reference such as `[ref=e4]`:

```
form
  textbox "Email" [ref=e1] [required] value=""
  button "Send" [ref=e4]
link "Docs" [ref=e5] -> /docs.html
```

The short commands act on the current tab and use the element references from the last outline they printed.

```
myarc open <url>             # open a tab in the Agent Space and print its outline
myarc snapshot [-i]          # print the outline; -i keeps only lines you can act on, with context
myarc click @e4              # click an element
myarc fill @e1 "text"        # replace a text field's value
myarc select @e3 "Pro"       # pick an option by value or visible text
myarc press Enter [@e1]      # send Enter, Tab, Escape, an arrow or one character
myarc back | forward | reload
myarc close                  # close the current tab
myarc tabs                   # list Agent Space tabs; * marks the current one
myarc use t12                # make another tab current
```

Every action prints a status line, what changed and the new outline, so you rarely need `snapshot` after a step. After a page navigates, references start again at `e1`, so always take them from the latest outline.

Options that work with every short command:

- `--tab t12` and `--rev 1.2` act on another tab or outline revision for one call.
- `--json` prints the raw response.
- Put `--` before text that starts with a dash, as in `myarc fill @e1 -- "-5"`.

Only http and https pages open. There is no scroll or wait command yet. `click` scrolls its target into view first, and if a page is still loading, run `snapshot` again.

## Exit codes

| Code | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| 0 | Success |
| 1 | The command returned an error, such as `stale` for an outdated reference |
| 2 | The command line was wrong |
| 3 | myArc isn't running, or browser control is off |
| 4 | myArc refused control, for example because you chose Don't allow |

Errors go to stderr. On `stale`, run `myarc snapshot` and use the new references. On `outcome_unknown`, the action may or may not have happened, so read the page before you try again.

## Run any command

`myarc commands` lists every command that works. `myarc run` sends one of them with JSON parameters:

```
myarc run space.list
myarc run space.create '{"name":"Work"}'
myarc run space.rename '{"space_id":1,"name":"Home"}'
```

These commands work today:

- Spaces: `space.list`, `space.create`, `space.select`, `space.rename` and `space.ensure_agent`, which creates the Agent Space if it's missing.
- Tabs in the Agent Space: `tabs.list`, `tab.open`, `tab.activate`, `tab.close`, `tab.navigate`, `tab.back`, `tab.forward` and `tab.reload`.
- Pages: `page.snapshot`, `page.click`, `page.fill`, `page.select` and `page.press`.

The Space commands reach all your Spaces in that Profile, so `space.rename` can rename one of yours. The first command runs in the window you used last. Later commands stay in that window's Profile until you turn control off or quit myArc.

## Use it from an MCP client

`myarc mcp` starts the MCP server. It has one tool per command, named with an underscore in place of each dot, so `space.create` is called `space_create` there. To add it to Claude Code for every project, run:

```
claude mcp add --scope user myarc -- "/Applications/myArc Nightly.app/Contents/Helpers/myarc" mcp
```

For other MCP clients, use this server entry once `myarc` is on your `PATH`:

```
{"command": "myarc", "args": ["mcp"]}
```

## Claude Code skill

The repository has a [Claude Code skill](https://github.com/bitbonsai/myarc/tree/main/skills/myarc-browser) that teaches Claude Code to drive myArc through the short commands. Copy the `skills/myarc-browser` folder into `~/.claude/skills/`.

## How tools connect

While control is on, myArc publishes its connection details in `~/Library/Application Support/myarc/control/`. Only your user account can read that folder. Tools connect over a local socket with a token that changes each time myArc starts. Nothing listens on the network.

[Next: Known limitations →](https://myarc.dev/docs/known-limitations/)

HTML: https://myarc.dev/docs/known-limitations/

# Known limitations

What the pre-alpha nightly can't do yet, and what to do after a crash or when something breaks.

myArc is a pre-alpha. Use it to try the Arc-style sidebar, and keep daily and sensitive browsing in another browser for now.

## Safety and updates

- Each nightly is built from a Chromium 158 development revision, before Chromium ships it as a stable release.
- There are no automatic updates and no security updates. Install each new nightly by hand, as [Install myArc](https://myarc.dev/docs/install/) describes.
- The app is signed with an Apple Developer ID but not yet notarized by Apple, so macOS blocks the first launch until you allow it.
- The protections around private windows, Profile separation, cookies and saved passwords aren't verified yet.
- Safe Browsing doesn't scan RAR downloads, because the UnRAR license conflicts with GPL-3.0, the license myArc uses.
- myArc is an independent project with no ties to Arc or The Browser Company.

## Video and media

- There is no Widevine, the copy protection that Netflix, Spotify and Disney\+ need, so those services won't play.
- H.264 and AAC are included, so most other web video plays.

## What doesn't work yet

- Arc Favorites arrive as pinned tabs in their Space, because the export doesn't mark them.
- Folders inside folders, and dragging a tab up to pin it or into a folder.
- Peek, Split View and Little Arc.
- Boosts and the Mini Player.
- The animated onboarding.
- The Links and Shortcuts tabs in Settings.
- Only the dark appearance has been compared with Arc. Light mode, Reduce Transparency and full-screen layouts haven't been checked.

## After a crash

Recent tabs and navigation can be lost after a crash or a force quit. Pinned tabs, Favorites and Spaces are saved in your workspace file, which [Your data](https://myarc.dev/docs/your-data/) describes, but whether every change survives a force quit isn't fully tested yet.

If a single page crashes, reload it with Cmd\+R. The rest of the browser keeps running.

Crash report uploads are off. Chromium keeps crash reports on your Mac, in `~/Library/Application Support/myArc Nightly/Crashpad/`. They can hold pieces of the pages you had open, so don't attach them to a public issue.

## Troubleshooting

### macOS won't open myArc

Each new download is blocked on its first launch. Follow the first-launch steps in [Install myArc](https://myarc.dev/docs/install/).

### macOS keeps asking for your password

myArc needs it to read the key that protects its saved data. Choose Always Allow. Nightlies before 2026.11.03 used a different signature, so moving from one of those asks once more.

### An agent says myArc can't be reached

The `myarc` command exits with code 3 when myArc isn't running or browser control is off. Start myArc and turn on Allow agents to control myArc in Settings \> Advanced. [CLI and MCP](https://myarc.dev/docs/cli-and-mcp/) has the details.

## Report a problem

Open an issue on [GitHub](https://github.com/bitbonsai/myarc/issues). Include the myArc version, shown at the top of the app menu next to the Apple menu, your macOS version and the steps that cause the problem. Leave out private pages.

# Letting agents use myArc

November 10, 2026

[Mauricio Wolff](https://github.com/bitbonsai)5 min read

myArc is built by agents. I lead a group of them that write the code, review it and test it. They could launch myArc and take screenshots of it, but they couldn't click anything in it. When they needed to browse, they used [agent-browser](https://github.com/vercel-labs/agent-browser), Vercel's browser tool for agents. I work with it and I like it, but it drives its own copy of Chrome, empty and off to the side. They were building a browser they couldn't use.

I wanted the same thing inside myArc, so this round I asked them to build it. An agent like Claude Code can now open pages in myArc, read them and click through them, in a Space of its own.

## Reading a page without looking at it

Many AI tools that use a computer work from screenshots. The model gets a picture of the screen, guesses where the button is and clicks at those coordinates. It works, but every step sends a whole image, and if the guess is a few pixels off, the click hits something else.

myArc borrows agent-browser's approach and hands the agent a short text outline of the page instead, with one heading, link, field or button per line. Everything the agent can act on gets a number. To sign up on a form, the agent fills `e1` with an email address and clicks `e2`. After each action it gets a fresh outline back, so it sees what changed without asking.

[![A terminal running three myarc commands. open prints a Sign up page outline with an Email textbox marked ref e1 and a Send button marked ref e2. fill e1 prints the same outline with the email filled in. click e2 reports that the tab navigated and prints a Thanks heading.](https://myarc.dev/blog/agents-use-myarc/agent-session.5a113358ee40.webp)](https://myarc.dev/blog/agents-use-myarc/agent-session.5a113358ee40.webp)

A sample session on a test page, drawn in the tool's real output format.

In the agents' test runs an outline came to a couple hundred characters per step. Each number stays tied to one element, so if the page changed under the agent, myArc refuses and the agent reads it again rather than clicking whatever now sits in that spot. Page text can't pass itself off as a button either, because whatever a page says comes back in quotes.

The agent gets in through `myarc`, a small command-line tool that also runs as an MCP server, the common way AI apps plug in outside tools. It works in its own Agent Space, the bot icon in the sidebar footer, and its pages load in the background while you keep browsing. Your other Spaces and Profiles stay out of its reach.

## The click that crashed

The agents started testing right away, and soon one of their clicks crashed the page. It only happened sometimes, after the agent had sat idle for a bit. For a while it looked like nothing was writing a crash report, until it turned out Chromium had saved every one, all pointing at the same spot in its code.

The bug was Chromium's own. Before a click, the browser checks where the element sits so it can scroll it into view, and that check read the page layout without updating it. A tab you're looking at redraws every frame, which keeps its layout fresh. The agent's tab sits in the background and doesn't draw, so its layout went stale, and a safety check stopped the page. The fix is one line that updates the layout first, as the function next to it already did. After that, the same test clicked through every round.

## Who gets to drive

With clicks working, the next question was how much an agent should be allowed to do without asking you. My answer is nothing, until you turn it on in Settings.

[![The Advanced tab of myArc's settings, with a Browser control section and an "Allow agents to control myArc" switch turned off](https://myarc.dev/blog/agents-use-myarc/browser-control-setting.d013fb5f9fcd.webp)](https://myarc.dev/blog/agents-use-myarc/browser-control-setting.d013fb5f9fcd.webp)

The switch starts off, and nothing can connect until you flip it.

The first time a tool connects, a card names it and asks whether it may control your Agent Space. Allow lasts until you quit myArc.

[![A myArc window with six Favorite tiles in the sidebar and a card at the top right reading "myarc 2026.11.13 wants to control your Agent Space", with Don't allow and Allow buttons](https://myarc.dev/blog/agents-use-myarc/connect-prompt.ebca1da71152.webp)](https://myarc.dev/blog/agents-use-myarc/connect-prompt.ebca1da71152.webp)

The card says what the tool can do and that it can't see your other Spaces.

The card can't prove who is asking, though. Each tool names itself when it connects, so another program on your account could claim to be `myarc`. You get to say yes or no and see the name it gave, and that's all.

While an agent works, a blue dot sits on the bot icon and a Stop button appears next to the Agent Space's name. Stop cuts it off at once, and the next time it connects, myArc asks again. Claude Code also gets a skill that teaches it the commands and tells it to check with you before it sends, buys or posts anything.

[![The top of the Agent Space in the sidebar, with a Stop button beside the Agent name and two Example Domain tabs below](https://myarc.dev/blog/agents-use-myarc/agent-space-stop.f7ac8431e496.webp)](https://myarc.dev/blog/agents-use-myarc/agent-space-stop.f7ac8431e496.webp)

The Agent Space while a tool is working.

## A sidebar full of globes

When the agents opened their test windows, I noticed every pin was a gray globe. myArc only learned a site's icon when you visited it, and those test profiles had never visited anything. After an import from Arc, everyone would have seen the same thing.

Now a pin without an icon asks its own site for one in the background and keeps it. The request sends no cookies, asks only for the site's home page, never the page you pinned, and goes straight to that site with no Google in between.

[![Six Favorite tiles in the sidebar showing the GitHub, Wikipedia, MDN, Hacker News, Rust and Python icons](https://myarc.dev/blog/agents-use-myarc/pin-icons.d8174aba615e.webp)](https://myarc.dev/blog/agents-use-myarc/pin-icons.d8174aba615e.webp)

None of these sites was ever opened in this profile.

## Leaving Arc

That import is the part I've been waiting for. I've used Arc since 2023, and I'd rather not rebuild those Spaces by hand.

Arc can export your Spaces to a file, under `Settings > Advanced > Export Data`. In myArc, `Settings > Advanced > Import from Arc…` reads that file and shows what it will add before it writes anything, along with the line number of anything it couldn't read. Each Space comes over with its folders and pinned tabs, in Arc's order. Import the same file twice and the second time adds nothing.

[![A dialog titled Import from Arc that reads "Adds 4 Spaces, 1 folder and 19 pinned tabs", with a note that each Arc folder becomes a folder in its Space, Favorites become pinned tabs and nothing opens until you click it, and Cancel and Import buttons](https://myarc.dev/blog/agents-use-myarc/arc-import-preview.2779d9969415.webp)](https://myarc.dev/blog/agents-use-myarc/arc-import-preview.2779d9969415.webp)

The preview from a test export. Cancel leaves your Spaces as they were.

One thing doesn't make it across yet. The export doesn't say which links are Favorites, so they land as pinned tabs in each Space.

The agents that build myArc don't need a separate Chrome anymore. They browse in a Space next to mine, inside the browser they're building. All of this is in the nightly, if you'd like to give your own agent a Space too.

HTML: https://myarc.dev/blog/one-window-two-profiles/

[All posts](https://myarc.dev/blog/)

# One window, two profiles

November 06, 2026

[Mauricio Wolff](https://github.com/bitbonsai)4 min read

I started with a simple question. If I make a Work Space and a Personal Space in myArc, do they keep their logins apart? I assumed they did. They didn't, and Arc never worked that way either.

In Arc a Space is a way of sorting tabs, and a Profile is what keeps your cookies, logins, history and extensions apart. Several Spaces can share one Profile. That sounds odd until you notice you have a lot more topics than identities. Home, Reading and Travel all want the same Google account. Work wants a different one.

myArc had Spaces but only ever one Profile, so everything shared a single cookie jar. The latest nightly fixes that.

## Creating a Space

Creating a Space now happens in the sidebar, the way it does in Arc. You give it a name, pick an emoji or an icon, choose which Profile it belongs to, and give it a color.

[![The Create a Space panel with the Profile menu open, listing Default and work, then New Profile](https://myarc.dev/blog/one-window-two-profiles/profile-menu.0660f821c781.webp)](https://myarc.dev/blog/one-window-two-profiles/profile-menu.0660f821c781.webp)

The Profile menu lists every Profile, and New Profile… makes a new one right there.

[![The emoji picker open under the Space name field, with Emoji and Icon tabs, a search field and a grid of emoji](https://myarc.dev/blog/one-window-two-profiles/emoji-picker.d4d58c9bac68.webp)](https://myarc.dev/blog/one-window-two-profiles/emoji-picker.d4d58c9bac68.webp)

Each Space can have an emoji or an icon.

The theme picker is simpler than Arc's for now, nine colors and an opacity slider. Arc has a whole color wheel with gradients and grain, and that can come later.

[![The theme popover with nine color chips, pink selected, and an opacity slider at 60 percent](https://myarc.dev/blog/one-window-two-profiles/theme-picker.f935d069532e.webp)](https://myarc.dev/blog/one-window-two-profiles/theme-picker.f935d069532e.webp)

Picking a color tints the sidebar while you choose.

[![Two myArc windows side by side, one Space tinted blue and one tinted orange](https://myarc.dev/blog/one-window-two-profiles/two-themes.864970080dec.webp)](https://myarc.dev/blog/one-window-two-profiles/two-themes.864970080dec.webp)

Each Space keeps its own color.

## The hard part

Arc showed every Space from every Profile in one window, and switching from a Work Space to a Personal Space just slid the sidebar over. Chromium doesn't allow that. Every window belongs to exactly one Profile, along with its tabs, address bar and extensions.

I had agents look at three ways around it.

Putting tabs from different Profiles into one window would have meant patching hundreds of files across Chromium's interface. Way too much for a pre-alpha.

The second idea looked like the winner. Keep one Chromium Profile and give each myArc Profile its own storage area, so cookies and site data stay apart while the window never changes. Then the research came back. History, saved passwords and extensions would still be shared, so a page you opened at work would show up in your personal command bar. Fixing that meant copying Chromium's password and history stores, which is exactly the kind of thing I don't want to maintain.

I also wondered about wrapping a bare web view in something like Tauri, the way Arc put its own interface on top of Chromium. On macOS Tauri uses Safari's engine though, and a real Chromium shell would mean rebuilding the whole browser around it.

## What shipped

Each myArc Profile is a real Chromium Profile, so the isolation comes for free. When you click a Space from another Profile, myArc brings that Profile's window in at exactly the same position and size, and the usual Space slide covers the swap. The old window stays hidden behind it, ready for when you switch back.

To make that feel like one window, a lot of small things had to agree. The Dock icon brings back one window instead of a stack. Closing the window closes the hidden ones too, with their usual warnings. The Window menu only lists the one you can see, and relaunching brings back only the window that was showing.

Agents also wrote a test that sets cookies, local storage, a database and a service worker in one Profile, then checks that the other Profile sees none of it, both ways and after a relaunch. It also checks that history and extensions stay put.

## What's still rough

During a swap there's a single frame where the sidebar loses its color. The first switch into a brand-new Profile doesn't slide at all. And a few paths haven't been tried by a person yet, so if something feels off when you switch Profiles, I'd like to hear about it.

HTML: https://myarc.dev/blog/ungoogled-chromium/

[All posts](https://myarc.dev/blog/)

# Taking a few patches from ungoogled-chromium

November 04, 2026

[Mauricio Wolff](https://github.com/bitbonsai)3 min read

myArc's nightly now takes a handful of privacy changes from [ungoogled-chromium](https://github.com/ungoogled-software/ungoogled-chromium), a Chromium fork that exists to cut out the parts that talk back to Google. Its code is BSD-3-Clause, which lets me reuse it as long as I credit it. The credit is in [ATTRIBUTION.md](https://github.com/bitbonsai/myarc/blob/main/ATTRIBUTION.md) and in a comment at every edit.

I only took the pieces that fit myArc.

## Why not rebase on it

The obvious move would be to build myArc on top of ungoogled-chromium and be done. Two things stop me. It follows Chromium's stable releases, while myArc follows Chromium's main branch, so switching would move the whole project onto an older base. And it strips out the real Chrome Web Store, which people coming from Arc need for their extensions.

So I read through its flags and patches and cherry-picked.

## The four flags

Build flags are switches you set when Chromium gets compiled. These four now live in `browser/args-nightly.gn`:

- `disable_fieldtrial_testing_config` gives the nightly Chromium's stable feature defaults, instead of the experiments Chromium switches on for test builds.
- `enable_reporting = false` removes the Reporting API and Network Error Logging, which let sites collect error reports from your browser.
- `enable_remoting = false` removes the Chrome Remote Desktop host.
- `enable_hangout_services_extension = false` removes the built-in Hangouts services extension.

## The five patches

Flags only go so far, so I also adapted five of ungoogled-chromium's patches. Some of them change more than I wanted, so I kept only the parts I needed. Agents dry-ran each one against myArc's Chromium before it went in, and the nightly builds with all five.

- Chromium no longer asks Google's servers for the current time.
- No Domain Reliability beacons, the small reports Chromium sends Google when a connection to one of its sites fails.
- WebRTC text logs, which video calls can upload for debugging, are off by default.
- No bundled Privacy Sandbox attestations list, the list of ad companies allowed to use Chrome's built-in ad APIs.
- Manifest V2 extensions keep working. That's the older extension format that full ad blockers like uBlock Origin were built on, and Chromium now disables it.

## What I left out

Some of ungoogled-chromium's changes would hurt myArc, and others add little here.

- `disable-ai` deletes pieces of Reading mode and PDF text recognition along with the AI features. myArc keeps AI off by default instead, so those pieces still work.
- Google host detection mostly stops Chromium from sending Google's sites an experiments header, `X-Client-Data`. With stable feature defaults that header should already carry very little, and the patch touches hundreds of lines.
- The crash reporter patch wasn't needed. Uploads are already off in myArc's builds, and a pre-alpha needs its local crash dumps.
- The Web Store patches, domain substitution (rewriting Google domains across the whole source) and binary pruning would break the real Chrome Web Store and extensions.
- `mei-preload` drops the list of media sites allowed to autoplay with sound, so those sites would stay muted until you'd used them for a while.

So myArc talks back to Google a little less now, and the Chrome Web Store still works. ungoogled-chromium itself cuts much deeper. myArc wants something narrower, a browser Arc's people can move into with their extensions intact, and these patches fit inside that.


---

HTML: https://myarc.dev/blog/closer-to-arc/

[All posts](https://myarc.dev/blog/)

# Chasing Arc's details

November 01, 2026

[Mauricio Wolff](https://github.com/bitbonsai)4 min read

[![myArc's sidebar with the creation menu open above the "+" button, listing New Space, a greyed-out New Split and a highlighted New Tab](https://myarc.dev/blog/closer-to-arc/creation-menu.6b5d41985107.webp)](https://myarc.dev/blog/closer-to-arc/creation-menu.6b5d41985107.webp)

The new creation menu. New Split stays greyed out until split view works. `2026.11.01 nightly`.

New nightlies keep landing on the [download page](https://myarc.dev/download/). A nightly is a pre-alpha build I make from the main branch, so you can try myArc without compiling Chromium yourself, which is an 80,000-step build you don't want to run.

Most of the recent work came from recording Arc and myArc side by side. Any single frame looked close enough, but in motion myArc's sidebar and menus snapped into place where Arc's animate. I've been using Arc since 2023, so I feel these things before I can name them.

## Turning a feeling into numbers

"Feels off" is hard to hand to a coding agent, but a number is easy, so I gave the recordings to agents and had them measure how long each of Arc's animations takes. Arc hides its sidebar in about a tenth of a second, and its creation menu fades in over two frames. Those timings became the tasks.

`Cmd+S` now hides and shows the sidebar at Arc's pace, and it peeks back in when you move the pointer to the window's edge. The "\+" button opens Arc's creation menu instead of a plain macOS one. The footer is laid out like Arc's, and its buttons show a tooltip with their name and shortcut.

## The bug that emptied Spaces

The worst bug in older nightlies lost data. If you quit myArc and opened it again, every tab you hadn't pinned was gone and your Spaces came back empty. If you're on one, please update. Sorry about that.

myArc and Chromium disagreed about what to restore on launch, and myArc threw away the tabs it couldn't find. Now it restores your last session by default, and a tab that doesn't come back stays in the sidebar anyway. It loads when you click it.

## The Library fills in

The Library is Arc's panel for things that aren't tabs: Spaces, Downloads, Archived Tabs and a few more. Its button used to open a short menu, and now the whole sidebar turns into the Library.

Each Space gets a card with its pinned tabs. You can rename a Space from its card or drag cards to reorder your Spaces, and I keep doing it just to watch the other cards slide aside.

[![The Library's Spaces section with three Space cards, Everyday, Research and Reading, each listing synthetic pinned tabs, and the icon rail on the left](https://myarc.dev/blog/closer-to-arc/library-space-cards.ce64221778f8.webp)](https://myarc.dev/blog/closer-to-arc/library-space-cards.ce64221778f8.webp)

Space cards in the Library, filled with synthetic tabs. `2026.11.01 nightly`.

Tabs you close land in Archived Tabs, and tabs you ignore for 12 hours get archived for you, like in Arc. Hover the Library button and your latest downloads fan out above it, ready to open or drag into another app.

[![Two crops of the sidebar footer: at rest with no downloads showing, then with the downloads stack showing sample.zip above the Library button](https://myarc.dev/blog/closer-to-arc/downloads-stack.cf200385ecfd.webp)](https://myarc.dev/blog/closer-to-arc/downloads-stack.cf200385ecfd.webp)

The footer at rest, then with the downloads stack open. `2026.11.01 nightly`.

One place I stepped away from Arc on purpose is the Library's blue. Arc's looked too loud next to the rest of the sidebar, so myArc uses a softer one.

## How far from an alpha

Most of this work is about how myArc looks. How it behaves is further behind. The [parity register](https://github.com/bitbonsai/myarc/blob/main/docs/PARITY.md) lists 12 behaviors a release can't ship without, and none of them is fully proven yet. Honest, if a bit painful to write.

Some big pieces don't exist at all. myArc can't import your Arc workspace yet, there's no ad blocking, split view isn't wired up and there's no onboarding in the browser. So instead of putting a date on alpha, I wrote an [alpha checklist](https://github.com/bitbonsai/myarc/blob/main/docs/ALPHA.md) where each item says what done looks like.

## Why the details

I could ship features faster if I stopped caring how a sidebar hides. But a two-frame fade is a big part of why Arc felt so good to use, and it's the part I miss most. I wrote about [the joy of sweating tiny details](https://mauriciowolff.com/blog/joy) before. This is the same itch, only now it's a whole browser.

Next I'm working through that checklist, one item at a time. If you try a nightly and something feels off, tell me in an [issue](https://github.com/bitbonsai/myarc/issues), even if all you can say is "the sidebar feels slow". That's the kind of note that started this round.

See you in the next nightly.

# Why myArc is now GPL-3.0

October 29, 2026

[Mauricio Wolff](https://github.com/bitbonsai)2 min read

Today I switched myArc's license from MIT to GPL-3.0. Both are open-source licenses, and for anyone who just downloads and uses myArc nothing changes. They differ in what someone can do with the code after taking it.

## Why I changed it

myArc exists because Arc is being sunsetted. Arc's code was never open, so when its company moved on, the people who used it every day had no way to keep it going. I don't want myArc to end up in the same place.

Under MIT, anyone can take the code, change it and ship a closed browser without sharing a line. Under GPL-3.0, anyone who distributes a modified myArc has to publish their source under the same license. Forks are welcome, but they stay open, and their improvements are available to everyone, including this project.

## I don't plan to make money from it

MIT's main advantage for an author is that it keeps commercial doors open: you can sell a closed edition or a separate commercial license later. I don't want either. myArc is something I'm building because I want to keep browsing this way, and I'm sharing it so others can too. Giving up those options costs me nothing.

## What else it gets us

- **Code from other browsers.** Privacy-focused Chromium browsers such as [Helium](https://github.com/imputnet/helium) publish their patches under GPL-3.0. myArc can now borrow them, for example for ad blocking, without license conflicts.
- **Patent protection.** GPL-3.0 includes a patent grant: contributors can't later sue users over patents covering the code they contributed.

## What changes in practice

- Releases and commits before the switch stay available under MIT. GPL-3.0 applies from [this commit](https://github.com/bitbonsai/myarc/commit/3bb4d23) onward.
- New contributions are licensed under GPL-3.0. No contributor agreement is needed.
- Chromium and the other bundled components keep their own licenses, listed in [ATTRIBUTION.md](https://github.com/bitbonsai/myarc/blob/main/ATTRIBUTION.md).
- One Chromium component, the RAR decompressor used to scan downloaded archives, has a license that conflicts with the GPL. It's turned off from the 2026.10.29 nightly onward, so RAR files you download aren't scanned.

The full text is in [LICENSE](https://github.com/bitbonsai/myarc/blob/main/LICENSE).

HTML: https://myarc.dev/blog/building-in-public/

[All posts](https://myarc.dev/blog/)

# Building myArc in public

October 25, 2026

[Mauricio Wolff](https://github.com/bitbonsai)4 min read

[![Mauricio Wolff's Arc card, dated 25 March 2023, with three anniversary stamps](https://myarc.dev/blog/building-in-public/mauricio-wolff-arc.c739650f7b1d.webp)](https://myarc.dev/blog/building-in-public/mauricio-wolff-arc.c739650f7b1d.webp)

My Arc card, 2023\.

I started using Arc in 2023\. I like how its sidebar works. Spaces and named pinned tabs turn it into something closer to a desk than a strip of tabs, and the command bar gets me back to any of those tabs fast.

[Arc is being sunsetted](https://arc.net/). I didn't want to lose that way of browsing, so I asked myself the obvious question: why not make an open, private-first version of Arc, with AI as an option? That's how myArc was born. Right now it's a Chromium-based prototype, and this post is where I write down what I'm trying and what breaks along the way.

## What I want from it

I want to open myArc and start browsing without creating an account or paying for a subscription. Moving a workspace in or exporting it out should work the same way, on my own machine.

I also want it to be private. myArc won't send analytics about how you browse, and it won't create an identifier per install to track you with. History and workspace data stay on your disk by default. I haven't verified all of this yet, though. Chromium ships with its own defaults and network behavior, and before any release I need to go through them and check what actually leaves the machine.

I do want to know whether people try it. GitHub's aggregate download totals per release are enough for that. The website and download host may keep ordinary request logs, which I'll disclose separately.

## Trying Artcraft's way of working

I'm borrowing [Artcraft's public engineering practices](https://github.com/storytold/photocraft/blob/main/AGENTS.md) as a starting point. PhotoCraft's development guide separates those checks: model tests run on their own, and visual checks happen in the native app.

Moving the navigation controls into the sidebar broke startup and layout. Going back to Chromium's native controls fixed both.

The address field also lost keyboard focus when layout hid it and showed it again. Keeping it visible brought navigation back. The lesson for me is that any time those controls move, I recheck startup and keyboard navigation in the native app.

Chromium provides the browser services, and Rust handles the workspace logic that's ours. Agent tasks follow that line.

**Update, 30 October 2026:** the Artcraft method didn't pay off for a browser. myArc now uses a simpler [screenshot loop](https://github.com/bitbonsai/myarc/blob/main/docs/WORKFLOW.md): one Arc screenshot, one agent, a side-by-side check, then the next task.

Each coding agent gets a narrow job with a result I can check myself. Right now that's the Rust Spaces model and a workspace service owned by a Chromium Profile, while another agent wires that state into the native sidebar. A separate agent reviews the change, and its findings go back for another implementation pass. The lead agent then merges the Rust and Chromium pieces, builds the browser and looks at the native window.

## Keeping context between sessions

Working this way means every new agent starts without the last one's context. I've open-sourced two skills under bitbonsai for that: [context](https://github.com/bitbonsai/context) and [wrap](https://github.com/bitbonsai/wrap).

Context keeps the agent instructions and architecture notes current, so a new agent can tell Chromium's parts from myArc's, and plans from working code.

Wrap saves the gotchas from a session and writes a handover for the next one. That's how the startup and focus failures above feed into the next pass instead of getting rediscovered. Private and machine-specific notes stay out of the public repo.

[myArc's code is open source too](https://github.com/bitbonsai/myarc).

## Where the build is

Page navigation works, and so does the centered native command palette. What I'm going for today is an Arc-like empty window and a native nightly build, so people can try it without compiling Chromium themselves.
